Before you begin Create a Project A collection holds functions and the tables they write. The group it is created in decides which kind of function it can hold, and that is fixed for the collection's life. A source or destination collection also carries exactly one connection, and it is created together with that connection rather than separately. Step 1Create a data product collection, for transformers tdk collection create \ --proj finance \ --name reporting \ --group default \ --description "Reporting tables" A collection in default, or in any group you created, holds transformers and takes no connection. Passing --conn-file here is an error. Step 2Or create a source collection, with its connection tdk collection create \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-postgres.yaml --conn-file is required for sources and destinations. The CLI derives the group from the connection's direction, so --group acts as an assertion: a mismatch is an error rather than a preference. Step 3Confirm it exists tdk collection list --proj finance tdk collection get --proj finance --name sales_src tdk collection get prints a data product collection's type as Data Factory, which is the same thing the docs call a data product.

--storage-path is the logical prefix for the collection's artifacts, written as base_path in the API. Unset, it inherits the project's prefix, and the resolved value is readable as effective_base_path. Changing it later is not retroactive: existing data versions keep the path they were written under, and only new artifacts use the new prefix.

Register a function into the collection. A source collection takes publishers, a destination collection takes subscribers, and a data product collection takes transformers. See tdk collection create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection Deleting a collection deletes its functions and tables, and freezes functions elsewhere that read from it. It takes a typed confirmation. Step 1Check what depends on the collection tdk table list --proj finance --coll sales_src Functions in other collections that read these tables are frozen by the delete, so it is worth knowing which tables those are. Step 2Delete it tdk collection delete \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src --confirm takes the literal string delete.

The delete is a soft delete with a cascade, in this order: The collection row is renamed to deleted_<id>, which frees the original name for immediate reuse. Functions in other collections that depend on its tables are set to Frozen. A frozen function stays registered and stops running until it is re-registered against tables that exist. Its tables, triggers and dependencies are set to Deleted, and its own functions are set to Deleted. Scheduled cron and stage workers are stopped. After the commit, the connection's stored content is deleted on a best-effort basis. Function status is one of Active, Frozen or Deleted, so a frozen function is visible in a listing rather than silently gone. See tdk collection delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection tdk collection update changes a collection's name, its description, its storage path, or the connection it carries. What it cannot change is the collection's type or the group it belongs to: both are fixed at creation. Step 1Rename it, or change its description tdk collection update \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --new-name sales_source \ --description "Postgres sales tables" Renaming a source or destination collection renames its connection too, since the connection is named by the collection. Step 2Or replace the connection tdk collection update \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --conn-file conn-postgres-prod.yaml The connector kind is fixed for the collection's life, so the replacement document has to be the same kind. Pointing a publisher at a different database means a new connection of the same kind, not a different connector. Step 3Check the result tdk collection get --proj finance --name sales_source A request that changes nothing is rejected: The collection update request has nothing to update. When a rename and a connection change are passed together, the rename is applied first.

The collection's type, and therefore its group, are immutable. There is no command that moves a collection to another group, and CollectionUpdate carries no field for it. Changing connectors means deleting the collection and creating it again. --storage-path applies to new artifacts only. Existing data versions keep the path stamped at write time. See tdk collection update for the full option list.

Before you begin Register a Function Step 1Delete the function tdk fn delete --coll reporting --name summarize --confirm delete --confirm takes the literal word delete. Omit it and tdk prompts for it instead. Step 2Confirm it is gone tdk fn list --coll reporting

Deleting a function does not delete the tables it wrote. Other functions that depend on those tables are frozen — they stay registered and stop running until re-registered against tables that still exist — rather than deleted along with the function that produced them. See tdk fn delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection A function is a Python file and the function inside it, registered into a collection. The kind of function a collection accepts follows from the group it was created in: a source collection takes publishers, a destination collection takes subscribers, and a data product collection takes transformers. Step 1Register the function tdk fn register \ --coll reporting \ --path summarize.py::summarize \ --description "Rolls orders up by region" --path names the file and the function inside it as file.py::function_name. Re-register after every code change — tdk fn register creates a new function version each time. Step 2Confirm it exists tdk fn get --coll reporting --name summarize --show-history on tdk fn get lists every version the function has gone through, newest first.

tdk fn register rejects a name that already exists in the collection unless you pass --update, which registers the new code as the next version of the same function instead of erroring. tdk fn register \ --coll reporting \ --path summarize.py::summarize \ --update
--reuse-tables tells the registration to keep any of the function's output tables that already exist in the collection, rather than erroring because they are already there.

A function registers enabled by default. --enabled false at registration time, or tdk fn disable --coll <collection> --name <function> afterward, stops it from running without deleting it. tdk fn enable turns it back on.
Trigger the function or wait for whatever trigger it was given to fire it on its own. See tdk fn register for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project A group sits inside a project and holds collections. Which group a collection is created in fixes what that collection can hold, and that choice is permanent. Three groups exist in every project already: sources for publishers, destinations for subscribers, and default for transformers. A group you create yourself holds transformers too, so the reason to add one is organising a pipeline rather than unlocking anything new. Step 1Create the group tdk group create \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --description "Raw ingested data" --proj names the project the group belongs to, and can be omitted when a project is pinned. Collections created in bronze hold transformers, the same as default. Step 2Confirm it exists tdk group list --proj finance The three seeded groups are listed alongside it. System groups cannot be renamed or deleted.

Collections in a user-created group hold transformers, which default already does, so grouping is organisational. The medallion layout, bronze then silver then gold, is a common convention for naming the stages of a pipeline; it is a docs convention rather than something Tabsdata enforces.
documents.s: Why add a group at all

documents.t: Create a Collection in the group. See tdk group create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Group Deleting a group deletes the collections inside it. Like the other deletes, it takes a typed confirmation. Step 1Check what the group holds tdk collection list --proj finance --group bronze Every collection listed here goes with the group. Step 2Delete it tdk group delete \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --confirm delete --confirm takes the literal string delete. The three system groups cannot be deleted, so this only ever applies to a group you created.

The group's collections are deleted with it, along with their tables and functions. Functions in other collections that depended on those tables are frozen rather than deleted: they stay registered and stop running until they are re-registered against tables that exist. See tdk group delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Group tdk group update changes a group's name or description. The collections inside it are untouched, and so is what those collections are allowed to hold. Step 1Rename the group, or change its description tdk group update \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --new-name raw \ --description "Raw ingested data" --name is the current name and --new-name the replacement. Either --new-name or --description is enough on its own. Step 2Check the result tdk group get --proj finance --name raw The three system groups, default, sources and destinations, cannot be updated at all.

A collection's type follows from the group it was created in, and renaming the group does not revisit that. A collection created in sources still holds publishers after the group is called something else. See tdk group update for the full option list.
documents.s: What a rename does not change

documents.t: Before you begin Install Tabsdata Start a Server A project is the outermost resource within Tabsdata server and allows full isolation from workflows and resources in other projects. Step 1Create the project tdk project create \ --name finance \ --description "Subscription billing" --name starts with a letter and continues with letters, digits or underscores, up to 100 characters, and has to be unique on the server. --description is optional and capped at 200 characters. Step 2Confirm it exists and see its groups tdk project list tdk group list --proj finance The three seeded groups appear straight away. A collection created in sources holds publishers, one in destinations holds subscribers, and one in default or any group you add yourself holds transformers.

Most commands take --proj to say which project they act on. Pinning one makes it the default: tdk project pin --name finance Every later command then acts on finance unless it passes --proj explicitly.
documents.s: Pin it, so later commands need no --proj

documents.t: A project on its own holds nothing. Create a collection in one of its groups: Create a Collection. See tdk project create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project warning Deleting a project deletes all resources nested inside of it, including function code, execution logs, and table data. This action cannot be reversed. Step 1Check what the project holds tdk group list --proj finance tdk collection list --proj finance Step 2Delete it tdk project delete \ --name finance --confirm takes the literal string delete. Anything else, including y or yes, cancels the command and leaves the project standing.

Every group and collection in the project is deleted with it, along with the tables those collections held and the functions registered in them. The project's name is freed and can be reused immediately. See tdk project delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project tdk project update changes a project's name or its description. Both are metadata: renaming a project does not move, rebuild or re-path anything inside it. Step 1Rename the project, or change its description tdk project update \ --name finance \ --new-name billing \ --description "Subscription billing and dunning" --name names the project as it stands now; --new-name is what it becomes. Passing only --description changes the description and leaves the name alone. Step 2Check the result tdk project get --name billing A request that changes nothing is rejected rather than silently accepted, with The project update request has nothing to update.

The project keeps its id, its groups, its collections and their data. Anything referring to the project by id keeps working; anything referring to it by name, a pinned project or a script passing --proj, needs the new name. See tdk project update for the full option list.
documents.s: What a rename does not change

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project This tutorial shows how to set up an Amazon S3 publisher that reads one or more files out of an S3 bucket and writes them into one or more Tabsdata Tables What you’ll do Configure a connection to S3 Write and Register a Publisher Function Trigger the publisher function

A Connection is a resource that stores the configuration and credentials needed to access an external system. Publishers use the credentials stored in a connection to authenticate with AWS. Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type s3-file-in --file conn-s3.yaml This creates a connection document within your working directory under the file name specified in the --file cli command. Step 2Fill in the bucket, the region, and the credentials within the connection document tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn spec: bucket: 'acme-ingest' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional Fill in the bucket name, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key, and base path. Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in connection document (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-s3.yaml

the filled-in connection document must be attached to a collection that contains (or will contain) the function using the connection credentials. Step 4Bind connection to a new or existing collection Create a New Collection Attach to an Existing Collection tdk collection create --name hr_files --group sources --conn-file conn-s3.yaml tdk collection update --name hr_files --conn-file conn-s3.yaml
documents.s: Bind connection document to a collection

documents.t: Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_files.py 1from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src 3 4 5@publisher( 6 source=S3Src( 1 paths=["departments.csv", "employees.csv"], 8 ), 2 output_tables=["departments", "employees"], 10) 3def read_files(departments, employees): 4 return (departments[0], employees[0]) 1paths S3 paths to read. Each element positionally maps to a function argument on line 11. 2output_tables Tabsdata tables function output is written to. Each name maps positionally to data returned on line 12. 3function arguments Data ingested from S3, positionally mapped and represented as Python function arguments. 4return Data the function outputs, mapped positionally to output tables defined on line 9. Each entry in the paths parameter represents the data contained in the file or files at that S3 path. Each paths entry maps positionally to an argument in the function body. Because Tabsdata supports wildcard expansion, a path can match either a single file, represented as a single-element list of TableFrames, or multiple files, represented as a list containing one TableFrame for each matched file. Variables listed in the function body's return statement represent output data and map positionally to the Tabsdata tables declared in the output_tables parameter. Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll hr_files --path read_files.py::read_files

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Db2 CDC publisher captures row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) from a Db2 database using SQL Replication. Db2 SQL Replication captures changes into shadow CD (Change Data) tables that the ASN capture program (asncap) populates in the background, so tables names the CD tables rather than the original source tables — the connector resolves the source table from ASN.IBMSNAP_REGISTER automatically. A long-lived stream worker hands a flushed batch to the publisher on each rollover, so this uses @stream_publisher rather than @publisher. What you’ll do Configure a connection to Db2 Write and Register the Stream Publisher

Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type db2-cdc --file conn-db2-cdc.yaml Step 2Fill in the URI and credentials, and bind it to a collection tdk collection create --name sales_cdc --group sources --conn-file conn-db2-cdc.yaml

Step 3Build the stream publisher file locally read_sales_changes.py 1from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2CdcStreamSrc 3 4 5@stream_publisher( 6 source=Db2CdcStreamSrc( 1 tables=["ASN.TD_T__ORDERS", "ASN.TD_T__CUSTOMERS"], 2 start_from="tail", 9 ), 3 flush_interval_mins=2, 4 output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], 12) 5def read_sales_changes(orders, customers): 6 return (orders[0], customers[0]) 1tables Qualified cd_schema.cd_table names of the CD tables to track, not the source tables. 2start_from "tail" begins at each table's current watermark and never backfills. 3flush_interval_mins Fallback rollover window in whole minutes if the capture table's own threshold has not fired. 4output_tables One output table per tracked CD table, in the same order. 5function arguments One TableFramesSpec parameter per source slot, always array mode. No ctx parameter. 6return One frame per output table, the same order as output_tables. start_from also accepts "head" to replay each tracked CD table from the origin, or an explicit CommitSeqPosition(seq=...), TableCommitSeqPosition(seqs={...}), or TimestampPosition(ts=...). A stream publisher takes no trigger_by and must not declare a ctx parameter — it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. documents.t: Rollover fires on whichever comes first: flush_interval_mins, or a threshold set via src_cfg, a config mapping over allowed CDC keys: src_cfg key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10,000 Flush to the working directory when row count in memory reaches this limit. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes None Flush when byte size in memory reaches this limit. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Flush when this many seconds have elapsed since the last flush. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_rows None Stage when total rows on disk reach this limit. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_bytes None Stage when total bytes on disk reach this limit. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_secs 60 Stage when this many seconds have elapsed since the last stage. tabsdata.cdc.poll_interval_seconds — Seconds between polling the CD tables for new changes. db2.cdc.blocking_timeout_seconds — Timeout in seconds for blocking reads. db2.cdc.fetch_size — Server-side fetch size for reading CD table rows. db2.cdc.logging_level — Log level for the capture reader. source=Db2CdcStreamSrc( tables=["ASN.TD_T__ORDERS"], start_from="tail", src_cfg={"tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows": 5000}, )
columns_format (default "columns", or "struct" / "map") and flatten_columns (default True) control how the new — and, where present, old — column values lay out on each emitted change row.

TRUNCATE TABLE operations are not captured. All CD tables must exist before the stream publisher is registered; the connector does not perform runtime table discovery. Schema changes on tracked tables are supported, but performing one on a table with CDC enabled is a complex administration effort on the Db2 side. Stop the stream publisher while schema changes are being made.
Refer to the IBM Db2 documentation for comprehensive and up-to-date configuration instructions.

SQL Replication requires archive logging so the capture agent can read the recovery log. mkdir $HOME/archive mkdir $HOME/backup db2 UPDATE DB CFG FOR sales USING logarchmeth1 disk:$HOME/archive/ db2 BACKUP DB sales TO $HOME/backup/ A full backup is required after enabling archive logging.

The ASN control tables store capture metadata. Create them using the asnclp tool: asnclp << EOF SET SERVER CAPTURE TO DB sales; SET CAPTURE SCHEMA SOURCE ASN; CREATE CONTROL TABLES FOR CAPTURE SERVER; EOF
asncap capture_server=sales capture_schema=ASN & The capture agent must be running before the connector can capture changes.

asnclp << EOF SET SERVER CAPTURE TO DB sales; SET CAPTURE SCHEMA SOURCE ASN; SET RUN SCRIPT NOW STOP ON SQL ERROR ON; CREATE REGISTRATION ( sales_schema.orders ) DIFFERENTIAL REFRESH IMAGE BOTH PREFIX _ CAPTURE ALL; EOF Option Description DIFFERENTIAL REFRESH Only changed rows are captured, not full table snapshots. IMAGE BOTH Both before-image and after-image are recorded for updates. PREFIX _ Before-image column names are prefixed with underscore. CAPTURE ALL All column changes are captured.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The grok function is a powerful log parsing tool for TableFrames that extracts structured data from log files and similar text formats. Originally developed for log analysis, it transforms a single text column into multiple typed columns by applying grok patterns with named captures. Grok is based on the Elasticsearch implementation and follows the same pattern syntax. For comprehensive pattern documentation, see the official Elasticsearch Grok documentation and the predefined pattern library. Grok uses regular expressions with predefined patterns to parse text. Each pattern includes named captures that become columns in your result. The function takes three inputs: Column Expression: Any expression that selects one column containing text to parse Pattern: A grok pattern string with named captures Schema: A mapping that defines output column names and data types for each capture While not technically a full-fledged connector like S3, Postgres, or Databricks, the grok log parser can be used with Publishers for Local File Systems and Object Storage in order to parse and convert single column logs into structured, tabular data. Each element positionally maps to a function argument on line 12. 2output_tables Tabsdata tables function output is written to. Each name maps positionally to data returned on line 13. 3function arguments Data read from the local filesystem, positionally mapped and represented as Python function arguments. A path with no glob arrives as a single-element list; departments.csv matches exactly one file, so departments[0] is that file. A glob can match several, so employees is concat()-ed into one table. 4return Data the function outputs, mapped positionally to output tables defined on line 10. Each entry in the paths parameter represents the data contained in the file or files at that local path. Each paths entry maps positionally to an argument in the function body. Since each output table takes exactly one TableFrame, a publisher combines a multi-file match with concat() before returning it; a single-file match just needs [0] to unwrap the list. Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project note The MySQL CDC connector needs a database driver that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. See Installing Third-Party Database Drivers for how to declare it during installation. The MySQL CDC publisher captures row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) from a MySQL database by reading its binary log (binlog) in real time. A long-lived stream worker follows the binlog and hands a flushed batch to the publisher on each rollover, so this uses @stream_publisher rather than @publisher. What you’ll do Configure a connection to MySQL Write and Register the Stream Publisher

Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type mysql-cdc --file conn-mysql-cdc.yaml Step 2Fill in the URI and credentials, and bind it to a collection tdk collection create --name sales_cdc --group sources --conn-file conn-mysql-cdc.yaml The connection holds the URI and credentials for MySQLCdcStreamSrcConn, which is separate from the batch MySQLSrcConn connector: it also reserves a server_id, the replica identifier the binlog stream uses. Each concurrent CDC connection against the same MySQL server needs a distinct server_id.

Step 3Build the stream publisher file locally read_sales_changes.py 1from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLCdcStreamSrc 3 4 5@stream_publisher( 6 source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc( 1 tables=["sales.orders", "sales.customers"], 2 start_from="tail", 9 ), 3 flush_interval_mins=2, 4 output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], 12) 5def read_sales_changes(orders, customers): 6 return (orders[0], customers[0]) 1tables Qualified schema.table names to track. 2start_from "tail" begins at the current binlog position and never backfills. 3flush_interval_mins Fallback rollover window in whole minutes if the binlog's own threshold has not fired. 4output_tables One output table per tracked table, in the same order. 5function arguments One TableFramesSpec parameter per source slot, always array mode. No ctx parameter. 6return One frame per output table, the same order as output_tables. start_from also accepts "head" to begin at the oldest retained binlog, or an explicit GtidPosition(gtid=...), BinlogPosition(file=..., pos=...), or TimestampPosition(ts=...). A stream publisher takes no trigger_by and must not declare a ctx parameter — it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. Step 4Register the stream publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sales_cdc --path read_sales_changes.py::read_sales_changes
documents.s: Write and Register the Stream Publisher

documents.t: Rollover fires on whichever comes first: flush_interval_mins, or a threshold set via src_cfg, a config mapping over allowed CDC keys: src_cfg key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10,000 Flush to the working directory when row count in memory reaches this limit. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes None Flush when byte size in memory reaches this limit. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Flush when this many seconds have elapsed since the last flush. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_rows None Stage when total rows on disk reach this limit. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_bytes None Stage when total bytes on disk reach this limit. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_secs 60 Stage when this many seconds have elapsed since the last stage. tabsdata.cdc.poll_interval_seconds 1 Seconds between polling cycles when no new events are available. mysql.cdc.blocking_timeout_seconds 1 Timeout in seconds for blocking reads from the binlog stream. mysql.cdc.logging_level — Log level for the binlog reader. source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc( tables=["sales.orders"], start_from="tail", src_cfg={"tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows": 5000}, )
columns_format (default "columns", or "struct" / "map") and flatten_columns (default True) control how the new — and, where present, old — column values lay out on each emitted change row.

TRUNCATE TABLE operations are not captured. All tables must exist in the source database before the stream publisher is registered. Tables created afterward are not captured. Schema changes on tracked tables (ALTER TABLE, ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN) are picked up automatically.
Refer to the MySQL documentation for comprehensive and up-to-date configuration instructions.

Add the following to your MySQL configuration file (my.cnf or my.ini) and restart the server: [mysqld] server-id = 1 log_bin = mysql-bin binlog_format = ROW binlog_row_image = FULL gtid_mode = ON enforce_gtid_consistency = ON Parameter Description server-id Enables binary logging with a unique server identifier. binlog_format = ROW Row-based format captures individual column values rather than SQL statements. binlog_row_image = FULL Logs all columns for every change, not just modified ones. gtid_mode = ON Required for resuming from a precise position across server restarts.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project note The PostgreSQL CDC connector needs a database driver that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. See Installing Third-Party Database Drivers for how to declare it during installation. The PostgreSQL CDC publisher captures row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) from a PostgreSQL database using WAL logical replication, decoded by the wal2json output plugin. Postgres logical replication requires a replication slot — a persistent cursor on the WAL the database will not garbage-collect until the consumer confirms. A long-lived stream worker hands a flushed batch to the publisher on each rollover, so this uses @stream_publisher rather than @publisher. What you’ll do Configure a connection to Postgres Write and Register the Stream Publisher

Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type postgres-cdc --file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml Step 2Fill in the URI and credentials, and bind it to a collection tdk collection create --name sales_cdc --group sources --conn-file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml PostgresCdcStreamSrcConn mirrors the batch PostgresSrcConn for the URI and credentials, but the connecting role must carry the REPLICATION attribute. The replication slot and publication live on the publisher's source object instead of the connection, so one connection can front several sources as long as each uses a distinct slot.

Step 3Build the stream publisher file locally read_sales_changes.py 1from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc 3 4 5@stream_publisher( 6 source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( 1 tables=["sales.orders", "sales.customers"], 2 replication_slot="sales_cdc_slot", 3 replication_slot_behavior="create", 4 start_from="tail", 11 ), 5 flush_interval_mins=2, 6 output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], 14) 7def read_sales_changes(orders, customers): 8 return (orders[0], customers[0]) 1tables Qualified schema.table names to track. 2replication_slot Logical replication slot this source attaches to. 3replication_slot_behavior "create" makes the slot if missing; "reuse" (default) requires it to already exist. 4start_from "tail" begins at the current WAL position and never backfills. 5flush_interval_mins Fallback rollover window in whole minutes if the WAL's own threshold has not fired. 6output_tables One output table per tracked table, in the same order. 7function arguments One TableFramesSpec parameter per source slot, always array mode. No ctx parameter. 8return One frame per output table, the same order as output_tables. start_from also accepts "head" to replay from the oldest retained WAL, or an explicit LsnPosition(lsn=...). A stream publisher takes no trigger_by and must not declare a ctx parameter — it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. Step 4Register the stream publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sales_cdc --path read_sales_changes.py::read_sales_changes
documents.s: Write and Register the Stream Publisher

documents.t: Rollover fires on whichever comes first: flush_interval_mins, or a threshold set via src_cfg, a config mapping over allowed CDC keys: src_cfg key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10,000 Flush to the working directory when row count in memory reaches this limit. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes None Flush when byte size in memory reaches this limit. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Flush when this many seconds have elapsed since the last flush. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_rows None Stage when total rows on disk reach this limit. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_bytes None Stage when total bytes on disk reach this limit. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_secs 60 Stage when this many seconds have elapsed since the last stage. postgres.cdc.blocking_timeout_seconds — Timeout in seconds for blocking reads from the replication stream. postgres.cdc.wal2json_format_version — wal2json output format version. postgres.cdc.logging_level — Log level for the replication reader. source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( tables=["sales.orders"], replication_slot="sales_cdc_slot", start_from="tail", src_cfg={"tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows": 5000}, )
columns_format (default "columns", or "struct" / "map") and flatten_columns (default True) control how the new — and, where present, old — column values lay out on each emitted change row.

TRUNCATE TABLE operations are not captured. All tables must exist in the source database before the stream publisher is registered. Schema changes on tracked tables (ALTER TABLE, ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN) are picked up automatically. Abandoned replication slots cause unbounded WAL growth. Monitor slot lag via pg_replication_slots and drop unused slots promptly.
Refer to the PostgreSQL documentation for comprehensive and up-to-date configuration instructions.
Add the following to postgresql.conf and restart the server: wal_level = logical max_replication_slots = 4 # at least 1 per CDC consumer max_wal_senders = 4 # at least 1 per CDC consumer

The wal2json extension must be installed on the PostgreSQL server. On Debian/Ubuntu, it is available as a system package: # Adjust version number to match your PostgreSQL version apt-get install postgresql-17-wal2json For installation instructions and detailed documentation, see the wal2json project.

Every Salesforce object carries a SystemModStamp column, and Tabsdata reads it to publish only the rows that changed since the previous run. Two things have to be true for that to work: SystemModStamp appears in the SELECT list, and the WHERE clause compares it against the $lastModified placeholder. On the first run $lastModified takes the value of initial_last_modified. On every later run it takes the highest SystemModStamp seen so far, so each trigger reads forward from where the last one stopped. Deletions are invisible to that comparison, because a deleted row stops appearing rather than getting a newer timestamp. Set include_deleted to True to read deleted records too, which is what makes an incremental load able to tell that a row went away.

Parameter Required What it does queries yes SOQL queries, one per output table, in order initial_last_modified no Starting timestamp for the first incremental run include_deleted no Reads deleted records as well. Defaults to False instance_url no Disambiguates the org when the credentials map to several version no Salesforce API version. Defaults to the latest

A query that returns no rows fills its slot with None rather than an empty frame. Returning None for a table tells Tabsdata to keep the previous version as current instead of committing a new one, which is the usual outcome of an incremental run with nothing new to read: read_when_available.py @publisher( source=SalesforceSrc( queries=["SELECT Id, Email, SystemModStamp FROM Contact " "WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified"], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000+0000", ), output_tables=["contacts"], ) def read_when_available(contacts): if contacts is None: return (None,) return (contacts[0],)

Authentication fails. Check that the username is the Salesforce username and not the email address, and that the security token matches the current password. Resetting either one invalidates the token. Every run re-reads everything. The query is missing $lastModified in its WHERE clause, or SystemModStamp is missing from the SELECT list. Both are required for the incremental read. Rows disappear from the source but stay in the table. include_deleted defaults to False, so deletions are not read at all. Wrong org. One set of credentials that maps to several orgs needs instance_url on the connection to pick between them.

reports takes one report or a list of them, referenced by id or by name. Which of the two is meant is inferred from the value, and find_report_by states it outright when the inference would guess wrong. A report referenced by name uses what Salesforce calls the report unique name, also shown as the developer name, rather than the label displayed in the UI. column_name_strategy decides where the output column names come from. A Salesforce report carries both a columnName and a label for every column: CREATED_ALIAS against alias, for instance. The choice sets the column names in the resulting Tabsdata table, and it also sets the names the filters have to use, so a filter written against labels breaks when the strategy is columnName.
documents.s: Naming a report, and naming its columns

documents.t: Each filter is a tuple of a column, an operator, and a value, in the form Salesforce report queries already use. More than one filter goes in a list. filter_logic states how those filters combine, referring to them by position: the first filter in the list is 1, the second is 2, and so on. "1 or 2" accepts a row matching either, and "1 or (2 and 3)" groups them. Without filter_logic, the filters carry no stated relationship between them.

initial_last_modified sets where the first run starts, as a string in Salesforce datetime format with the timezone included. last_modified_column names the column the comparison runs against, and that column has to be in the report for the read to work. It defaults to None, which reads the whole report on every run.

Parameter Required What it does reports yes One report or a list, by id or by name column_name_strategy no columnName (default) or label, setting output column names find_report_by no id or name, when the reference is ambiguous filter no Tuples of column, operator, value filter_logic no How the filters combine, by position initial_last_modified no Starting timestamp for the first incremental run last_modified_column no Report column driving the incremental read

A filter matches nothing. Filters use whichever names column_name_strategy selected, so a filter written against alias fails under columnName and needs CREATED_ALIAS instead. The report is not found by name. Salesforce matches the report unique name, not the label in the UI. Set find_report_by to name and pass the unique name, or reference the report by id. Every run re-reads the whole report. last_modified_column is unset, or the column it names is missing from the report definition.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The ClickHouse connector is destination-only. It stages Parquet files in cloud storage and then loads them through ClickHouse table functions such as s3() or azureBlobStorage(). The connector currently supports S3, Azure Blob, and GCS staging. Each entry in tables takes one input table, in order, and writes it to that destination table. The connector ships separately from the core package: pip install 'tabsdata[clickhouse]' What you’ll do Configure a connection to ClickHouse Write and Register a Subscriber Function Trigger the subscriber function

The connection holds the server address, the credentials, and a staging block naming the cloud storage the load goes through. Combine rows from two or more Tabsdata Tables. A transformer declares one input_tables entry per table and takes a parameter for each.

concat() stacks TableFrames by appending their rows. how decides what happens when the inputs do not line up: verticalvertical_relaxeddiagonaldiagonal_relaxed The default, so it can be left off. Every input must share the same columns and the same types. concat.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @transformer( input_tables=["sales_east", "sales_west"], output_tables=["sales_all"], ) def transform(east: TableFrameSpec, west: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = concat([east, west]) return result sales_east region month amount east jan 10 east feb 20 2 rows sales_west region month amount west jan 30 west feb 40 2 rows sales_all region month amount east jan 10 east feb 20 west jan 30 west feb 40 4 rows note None entries in the list are skipped. A list that is None, empty, or empty once the None entries are dropped makes concat() return None, which leaves the output table on its current version instead of committing a new one. See concat for the full signature.
While TableFrames are typically received as input in publishers and transformers, you can also create them programmatically for testing or data generation purposes.

Use TableFrame.from_dict() to create a TableFrame from a Python dictionary: transform.py from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame data = { "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"], "age": [25, 30, 35], "city": ["New York", "London", "Paris"] } tf = TableFrame.from_dict(data)

A transformer reads one or more Tabsdata Tables and writes new Tabsdata Tables. Joining two of them is the most common case: declare both under input_tables and the function takes a parameter for each. See Transformers for the anatomy of a transformer Function. Every block below joins the same two tables. orders has three rows and customers has three, overlapping on two customer_id values: o3 points at c9, which no customer has, and c3 has no order. What a join does with those two rows is the whole difference between the types.

Set the type with how. Every one of these joins on customer_id: innerleftrightfullsemianti Only the rows that match on both sides. The default. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "customers"], output_tables=["order_names"], ) def transform(orders: TableFrameSpec, customers: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = orders.join(customers, on="customer_id") return result orders order_id customer_id amount o1 c1 10 o2 c2 20 o3 c9 5 3 rows customers customer_id name c1 Ada c2 Grace c3 Cy 3 rows order_names order_id customer_id amount name o1 c1 10 Ada o2 c2 20 Grace 2 rows

A key can span several columns, and the two sides can name them differently: on=[...]left_on / right_on One key spanning several columns. A row matches only when every column agrees. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["visits", "targets"], output_tables=["visits_vs_target"], ) def transform(visits: TableFrameSpec, targets: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = visits.join(targets, on=["customer_id", "date"]) return result visits customer_id date spend c1 mon 10 c2 mon 7 c1 tue 4 3 rows targets customer_id date target c1 mon 12 c2 mon 5 2 rows visits_vs_target customer_id date spend target c1 mon 10 12 c2 mon 7 5 2 rows

Before you begin Create a Project A CDC stream source reads a database's replication log and emits one Tabsdata table per tracked table. Every insert, update, and delete arrives, rather than whatever a SELECT happens to see when it runs. Three databases have a CDC source, each with its own connection type: Connection type Database Class mysql-cdc MySQL MySQLCdcStreamSrc postgres-cdc PostgreSQL PostgresCdcStreamSrc db2-cdc IBM Db2 Db2CdcStreamSrc What runs the publisher is a rollover rather than a clock or an upstream commit. The stream worker consumes the log continuously, and when a threshold trips it writes the buffer out and hands the batch to the publisher, which de-duplicates and offset-filters the rows before ingesting them. @stream_publisher takes no trigger_by. Step 1Create the connection tdk connection template --type mysql-cdc --file conn-cdc.yaml Fill in the URI, the credentials, and the tables list, then create the collection: tdk collection create \ --name inventory \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-cdc.yaml All three CDC types register with direction stream-src, which maps to the sources group. Step 2Write the stream publisher read_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLCdcStreamSrc @stream_publisher( source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc( tables=["shop.products", "shop.stock"], start_from="tail", ), flush_interval_mins=5, output_tables=["products", "stock"], ) def read_changes( products: TableFramesSpec, stock: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFramesSpec, TableFramesSpec]: return (products, stock) One output table per tracked table, in order, and one TableFramesSpec parameter per slot. The function must not declare a ctx parameter: it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. Step 3Register it tdk fn register \ --coll inventory \ --path read_changes.py::read_changes Registration starts the stream worker, which begins consuming the log.
documents.s: Trigger off CDC in an SQL Database

documents.t: start_from decides what the worker reads first. For PostgreSQL, "head" starts at the oldest retained WAL, "tail" starts at the current LSN, and an LsnPosition starts at a position you name. Starting at the tail skips the history and streams only what arrives from now on.

PostgreSQL logical replication is slot-based, so its connection carries fields the other two do not: Field Purpose replication_slot The slot name, required replication_slot_behavior "reuse" (default) or "create" publication_name Optional publication to read from columns_format "columns" (default), "struct", or "map" flatten_columns Defaults to True

flush_interval_mins is a fallback ceiling, minimum 1 whole minute. The connector's own thresholds in src_cfg cover buffer size and polling cadence, and whichever threshold trips first closes the batch, so the connector's window is usually the one that fires.

MySQL and PostgreSQL CDC both need a database driver that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. Declare it during installation, as described in Installing Third-Party Database Drivers. Adding it later means re-running the installation.
Trigger off a Kafka Stream covers the fourth stream source, which follows the same rollover model against a topic. See Stage Triggers for how a batch closes and becomes a run.

Before you begin Create a Project A CronTrigger runs a function at fixed times whether or not any upstream data changed. It is the right trigger for a publisher, which has nothing inside Tabsdata to signal that its external system has new rows. Tabsdata reads every crontab schedule in UTC. Step 1Add a CronTrigger to the function read_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import CronTrigger, TableFrameSpec, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc @publisher( source=MySQLSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM orders"], ), output_tables=["orders"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders "0 * * * *" fires at the top of every hour. The mask is standard 5-field crontab syntax, Minute Hour Day Month Day-of-Week, with minute precision. Extensions like @hourly and @daily are not supported. Mask When it runs 0,30 * * * * Every 30 minutes, on the hour and at minute 30 0 0 * * * Daily at 00:00 UTC 0 22 * * FRI Fridays at 22:00 UTC Step 2Register the function tdk fn register \ --coll sales \ --path read_orders.py::read_orders The schedule starts from the moment registration succeeds. Re-register with --update after any change to the mask. Step 3Confirm the schedule took tdk fn get --coll sales --name read_orders

start and end limit when the mask applies. Both take a timezone-aware Python datetime or an ISO 8601 string in UTC: trigger_by=CronTrigger( "0 * * * *", start="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", end="2026-04-01T00:00:00Z", ) Omit them and the mask applies indefinitely from registration.
documents.s: Bounding the schedule to a window

documents.t: A cron schedule only fires while its function is enabled, so pausing one is a matter of disabling the function rather than editing the mask: tdk fn disable --coll sales --name read_orders tdk fn enable --coll sales --name read_orders A disabled function keeps its registration and its mask, and Tabsdata ignores the mask until it is enabled again. Register a function --disabled to add it without starting its schedule.

A cron trigger fires on a clock regardless of upstream state. To run a function because data actually arrived, see Trigger a Function from a Table Commit. See Cron Triggers for how the trigger behaves.

Before you begin Create a Project A Kafka stream source consumes one topic continuously and emits a single Tabsdata table named after that topic. What runs the publisher is neither a clock nor an upstream commit but a rollover: the stream worker buffers messages, and when a rollover threshold trips it writes the buffer out as parquet and hands the batch to the publisher to ingest. @stream_publisher therefore takes no trigger_by at all. Step 1Create the connection tdk connection template --type kafka-topic-in --file conn-kafka.yaml Fill in the bootstrap servers, then create the collection with it: tdk collection create \ --name events \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-kafka.yaml servers is the only required field. credentials is optional, so a broker that takes SASL gets a UserPassword block here and a broker without authentication gets none. The topic is not a connection field: it belongs to the source in the function, along with the message format and schema. A Kafka connection registers with direction stream-src, which maps to the sources group like a plain source does. Step 2Write the stream publisher read_clicks.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.kafka import KafkaStreamSrc CLICK_SCHEMA = """ { "type": "record", "name": "Click", "fields": [ {"name": "user_id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "url", "type": "string"}, {"name": "ts", "type": "long"} ] } """ @stream_publisher( source=KafkaStreamSrc( topic="clicks", data_format="json", schema=CLICK_SCHEMA, ), flush_interval_mins=5, output_tables=["clicks"], ) def read_clicks(clicks: TableFramesSpec) -> TableFramesSpec: return clicks The output table takes the topic's name, and there is always exactly one. schema is required, and in schema-registry mode it is cross-checked against the registry. The function takes one TableFramesSpec per source slot, always in array mode, and must not declare a ctx parameter: it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction, so no transaction context exists at the call boundary. Step 3Register it tdk fn register \ --coll events \ --path read_clicks.py::read_clicks Registration starts the stream worker. It consumes continuously from that point.

Rollover fires on whichever threshold trips first, the connector's own or the decorator's fallback. Kafka takes min(time_rollover_secs, flush_interval_mins * 60), so flush_interval_mins is a ceiling and the connector's window is usually the one that fires. Set the connector's thresholds in src_cfg: Key Closes the batch when kafka.time_rollover_seconds That many seconds have passed kafka.size_rollover_mb The buffer reaches that size kafka.messages_rollover That many messages have accumulated flush_interval_mins takes whole minutes, minimum 1.
Set dlq_topic on the source and Kafka messages that cannot be deserialized are routed there instead of failing the batch.

Trigger off CDC in an SQL Database covers the other three stream sources, which follow the same rollover model against a database log. See Stage Triggers for how a batch closes and becomes a run, and Kafka for the full connector setup.

Before you begin Create a Project tdk fn trigger runs a registered function on demand. Any function can be triggered this way, including one that already carries a trigger_by schedule, so a manual trigger is how you test a function before trusting it to a cron mask. A publisher with no trigger_by runs only when triggered manually. That is the default for publishers, since nothing upstream inside Tabsdata can signal that an external system has new data. Step 1Trigger the function tdk fn trigger \ --coll sales \ --name read_orders The command waits for the plan to finish and reports each function as it completes. Pass --detach to return immediately instead. Step 2Check what the run produced tdk table list --coll sales tdk table data --coll sales --name orders

A trigger does not run one function in isolation. Tabsdata builds an execution plan covering every function downstream of the one you named, and runs them in dependency order: a transformer reading the publisher's output runs next, then a subscriber reading that transformer's output. Nothing commits unless every function in the plan succeeds. Name the plan to make it easier to find afterward: tdk fn trigger \ --coll sales \ --name read_orders \ --plan-name nightly-backfill
documents.s: Triggering runs more than one function

documents.t: tdk fnrun list --coll sales --fn read_orders The listing carries each run's id, which is what the log and recovery commands take: tdk fnrun logs --fnrun <run_id> tdk fnrun recover --fnrun <run_id> recover resumes the plan a failed run belongs to rather than starting a new one.

Automate it. Schedule a Cron Trigger runs the function on a clock, and Trigger a Function from a Table Commit runs it when an upstream table gets new data. See Manual Triggers for how the trigger behaves, and tdk fn trigger for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project A table trigger runs a function whenever a table it watches receives a new commit. This is how a pipeline advances on its own: a publisher lands data, the transformer watching that table runs, and the subscriber watching the transformer's output runs after it. Transformers and subscribers already work this way without being told to. Omit trigger_by and a commit to any of the function's input tables triggers it. trigger_by is for the two cases the default does not cover: triggering off fewer tables than the function reads, and triggering off tables it does not read at all. Step 1Write the function against its input tables summarize.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["orders"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], ) def summarize(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders.group_by("region").agg(col("amount").sum()) With no trigger_by, a commit to orders runs this transformer. Step 2Register it tdk fn register \ --coll sales \ --path summarize.py::summarize Step 3Trigger the upstream function and watch the chain tdk fn trigger --coll sales --name read_orders The publisher commits orders, which triggers summarize in the same execution plan. Both appear in the run listing: tdk fnrun list --coll sales
documents.s: Trigger a Function from a Table Commit

documents.t: A commit to any input table triggers the function, and trigger_by narrows that set: @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "regions"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], trigger_by=["orders"], ) regions is still read on every run and still supplies its current data. It no longer starts one, which suits a lookup table whose edits do not warrant recomputing the summary. This is not about avoiding duplicate runs. A plan that commits both orders and regions runs this transformer once either way, because the plan covers every downstream function and orders them by dependency rather than firing one run per committed table.

trigger_by accepts tables that are not inputs at all, which is how a function runs in response to something it does not consume. input_tables and trigger_by are two independent lists — one controls what the function reads, the other what starts it, and neither has to be a subset of the other: @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "regions"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], trigger_by=["orders", "ops/refresh_signal"], ) def summarize(orders: TableFrameSpec, regions: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders.group_by("region").agg(col("amount").sum()) regions is read on every run but never starts one, since it is absent from trigger_by. ops/refresh_signal starts a run despite never being read, since it is absent from input_tables. A commit to ops/refresh_signal runs the transformer even though it reads nothing from that table. A publisher uses the same mechanism: it has no input_tables at all, so a table reference in trigger_by is the only way a Tabsdata commit can start it. Reference a table outside the function's own collection as collection/table. Cross-collection references work within one project. A reference to a table in another project surfaces as Dependency table '<x>' does not exist, because row-level security hides it rather than reporting it as forbidden.
documents.s: Triggering off a table the function does not read

documents.t: An empty list disables it, leaving the function manual-only: trigger_by=[]

A publisher writing three tables commits all three on every run, whether or not the rows in a given table differ from last time, and every commit triggers whatever watches that table. A run that returns None for a table is the exception: that keeps the current version instead of committing a new one, so nothing downstream fires.
